questions.q: Why does this lesson say the Northgate Health Partners scenario deliberately doesn't map cleanly onto any single Chapter 1 case study?
options: Because it combines elements of a read-mostly external-system problem and a bidirectional-sync problem, testing whether the underlying workflow transfers to a new combination rather than a memorized pattern
Because it is actually identical to the Harborline Capital case study
Because Northgate Health Partners does not use Salesforce
Because mock review boards are not supposed to involve any new scenario
questions.explain: The scenario intentionally blends a Lesson-1-style external-system read problem with a Lesson-5-style bidirectional messaging problem, so the capstone tests whether the student can apply the workflow itself to something new, not recall a solved example.

questions.q: In the scoping step, why does this lesson recommend an event-driven update for appointment status rather than a nightly batch?
options: Because appointment status never actually changes
Because nightly batches are technically impossible to build in Salesforce
Because status changes a few times per appointment and staff need to see same-day changes like a cancellation, which a once-a-day batch would leave invisible for up to 24 hours
Because event-driven designs never have any failure modes to worry about
questions.explain: The moderate but same-day-relevant frequency of appointment-status changes is exactly the volatility profile that argues for an event-driven update, since a nightly batch would delay a same-day cancellation by up to a full day.

questions.q: In the mock reviewer exchange, what does the modeled answer about a Salesforce outage during a patient text reply honestly admit?
options: That the design has no gaps at all and handles every case perfectly
That the current design doesn't yet specify a maximum retry window or an alert for a message dropped after retries are exhausted -- a real, named gap rather than an overstated claim of coverage
That the text-messaging platform cannot technically send or receive any messages
That Salesforce availability is never a concern for any integration
questions.explain: The modeled answer explicitly names an unresolved gap (no stated maximum retry window or alerting after exhausted retries) instead of claiming the design already handles it -- directly modeling the honest-gap-admission standard from Lesson 12.

questions.q: How does the Northgate design match a patient's text reply to the correct Salesforce case?
options: By asking the patient to type their case number into every reply
By matching on the patient's phone number alone, with no other identifier
Replies are never matched to a case automatically under any circumstances
Using a reference ID included in the original outbound reminder message, echoed back in the reply thread by the text platform
questions.explain: The design embeds a reference ID in the outbound message, which the text platform echoes in the reply thread, allowing automatic matching back to the originating case -- with a stated limitation for replies outside that thread.

questions.q: What single habit does this lesson say it is modeling again in its mock reviewer exchange, as the course's capstone?
options: Giving the most accurate answer available under real questioning, including naming a genuine unresolved gap rather than overstating the design's coverage
Always claiming a design is complete and flawless under live questioning
Avoiding any mention of failure modes during a presentation
Refusing to answer any reviewer question that wasn't anticipated in advance
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly calls out that its second mock answer doesn't claim an unsolved problem is solved, reinforcing the course-wide standard from Lesson 12 of giving the most accurate answer available, including an honest admission of a real gap.
